r39.note: The request handler implements the demonstrated retry decision and skips custom processing on the marked request.
r39.intro: The Function handles a processing failure by redirecting the browser with ewresponse=retry. On that request the handler runs again, skips only the PIM processing step and continues to the backend.

r36.title: Who is allowed through the waiting room?
r36.note: Queue-it or equivalent through Routing Middleware is the proposed admission mapping; customer integration is not yet demonstrated.
r36.intro: The current waiting room controls access to checkout and login and remembers temporary visitor admission. Queue-it or an equivalent service would own that admission state. In our proposed Vercel mapping, a connector in Routing Middleware validates it before access to protected content and the application.
r36.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant V as Visitor browser
  participant M as Proposed Middleware connector
  participant Q as Queue-it
  participant A as Protected cache / application
  V->>M: Request protected path
  alt No valid admission state
    M-->>V: Redirect to Queue-it
    V->>Q: Follow redirect
    Q-->>V: Return with signed token when admitted
    V->>M: Request protected path with token
    M->>M: Validate token and create session cookie
    M->>A: Continue admitted request
    A-->>V: Response with session cookie
  else Valid session cookie
    M->>A: Continue admitted request
    A-->>V: Response
  end
r36.flow: Illustrative Queue-it server/edge connector flow. Routing Middleware is our proposed Vercel placement; it is not an explicit Queue-it recommendation for Vercel. The Argos integration has not been demonstrated.
paragraphs: R35 returns a holding response. R36 decides who may proceed and remembers that decision across requests. Queue-it supplies the waiting room and admission state; the connector checks protected paths and the visitor’s token or session cookie.

r27.intro: First establish whether the browser can connect directly to the existing chat backend. If the customer needs a relay through Vercel, a custom Function can accept one WebSocket and open a second to the backend; this bounded sample demonstrates forwarding, not that a relay is necessary.

r27.observation: 18 of 19 recorded checks passed. The platform cutoff remains unverified; the application timer is not evidence of the platform limit.
r27.detail: Official docs checked 27 September label Function WebSockets beta on all plans and require Fluid compute. They say connections close at Function maximum duration and clients must reconnect and restore state. That documented expectation conflicts with the bounded 30-second configuration test. It remains unresolved, not an unlimited-lifetime guarantee or a demonstrated inability to serve this customer. This owned project exercised Node v24.20.0 with Fluid compute; customer eligibility and architecture are separate. The demo does not establish transparent passthrough, all control frames/extensions, production load, durable session restoration or customer authentication. The 25-second application timer and 20-second idle probe are sample policies, not customer requirements.
r27.decision: Obtain the actual chat URL, authentication and session-recovery contract, then choose direct backend access or a two-connection relay and resolve its platform-duration behavior before relying on it.

r10.title: Can the response report the visitor’s actual TLS version and cipher?
r10.note: Exact visitor TLS/cipher unavailable in the tested interface; a supported authoritative source remains unconfirmed.
r10.intro: The response should report the TLS version and cipher negotiated between the browser and Vercel. Whether Vercel can populate those headers natively with the actual connection values still needs confirmation.
r10.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
 participant B as Browser
 participant V as Vercel
 B->>V: Negotiate HTTPS connection
 Note over B,V: TLS version and cipher selected for this connection
 B->>V: HTTPS request
 V-->>B: Required response headers: Akamai-TLS and Akamai-CIPHER
 Note over B,V: Desired behavior, native header population is unconfirmed
r10.flow: The requested headers describe this browser connection, not a connection from Vercel to an origin.
r10.observation: Strict certificate-verified client connections recorded their negotiated version and cipher. The Function socket was plaintext and had no getProtocol/getCipher methods; HTTPS and fingerprint signals did not establish the exact negotiated pair. In forged-header controls, Akamai-TLS and Akamai-CIPHER contained the caller’s FORGED values. Echoing those headers would not provide trustworthy diagnostics.
r10.detail: Documentation reviewed 27 September 2026 and the tested Function interface did not establish an authoritative source for the pair. Firewall JA3/JA4 hashes describe handshake fingerprints; they do not establish the exact selected pair required here. Both clean and forged-header tests used certificate-verified client sockets. This is an unmet outcome in the tested Function interface, with product-wide support still unconfirmed. Origin socket values, a user-agent guess or caller-supplied headers cannot substitute for visitor connection metadata.
r10.decision: Confirm whether native response-header configuration can use the negotiated visitor TLS version and cipher, and the exact supported interface. Missing Function access alone does not establish that native population is impossible.
